title: Ship Your Interpreter
excerpt: LLMs can write rules for a programming language and prove that its interpreter follows them.

Published: October 16, 2026

Article: Kiran Gopinathan, Nikhil Pimpalkhare, Yiyun Liu, Zenna Tavares

We had LLMs write precise mathematical rules, or a formal semantics, for how a small programming language should behave. We then used Lean, a tool for checking mathematical proofs, to prove that the interpreter—the program that runs code written in that language—follows those rules even after being compiled into low-level instructions understood by a RISC-V computer chip.

LLMs are growing alarmingly capable at finding and exploiting bugs in production software, with increasing reports of AI-assisted hacks in the wild. Fortunately, LLMs are advancing quickly in their ability to write verified software: programs that come with mathematical proofs, checked by a computer, that rule out entire classes of bugs. In April, our agents built a JavaScript-to-WebAssembly compiler but could not prove that it preserved program behaviour. Months later, our agents verified Linux’s nftables compiler, which translates firewall rules into instructions the kernel executes. In September, MIT researchers Frans Kaashoek and Nickolai Zeldovich used AI agents to verify the xv6 operating-system kernel down to its machine code.

Our goal at Basis is to develop verification methods that could plausibly scale to all software, so that the systems powering critical infrastructure are secure by design and keep pace with attackers’ growing capabilities. As LLMs advance in capability, the bottleneck is shifting away from theorem proving and towards the problem of specification: how can we be sure that the statements we prove capture the behaviour we actually care about?

To prove anything about a program, we first need a mathematical description of what it does. This starts with describing the programming language it is written in: what every statement, loop, and function call means when it runs. These descriptions are called a formal semantics, and can be written with pen and paper, but are increasingly expressed in a proof assistant such as Lean. A handful of languages have one (Standard ML, WebAssembly, and C via CompCert), as does the RISC-V instruction set that a growing number of processors execute. Developing each of these semantics took years of expert effort.

Most programs, however, are written in languages that do not have a formal semantics, presenting a major bottleneck for deploying verified software at scale: without a semantics, there is nothing precise to prove against. A natural solution is to use LLMs to write semantics, but LLMs make mistakes, and a broken semantics undermines every proof built on it. Testing helps, but as we show below, a semantics can pass every test and still be wrong. What is needed is a means to verify the semantics itself.

Languages without a formal semantics still have interpreters or compilers, which in practice define what their programs mean. Here we consider a radical idea: make the LLM prove that its semantics agrees with the real interpreter on every program, treating the interpreter as ground truth. To do this, we compile the interpreter to RISC-V, whose meaning is already formally defined. That gives an exact, if unreadable, description of what the interpreter does with any program. The LLM then writes readable rules for the language and proves in Lean that, for every possible program, those rules predict exactly what the compiled interpreter prints. If a rule is wrong, the proof gets stuck.

We report on an experiment where we had LLMs develop a semantics and its proof together for a small language. We used Lean to prove that the interpreter, the program that runs code written in that language, follows those rules even after being compiled into low-level machine instructions. The whole development, semantics and proof, is on GitHub. The rest of this post walks through this experiment, explaining first why semantics are the bottleneck for larger verification efforts and why tests aren’t sufficient to build trust in them. We then show how the proof process refined the semantics, how we handled the memory reasoning, and what tools we built on the result.

Every verified program starts from a semantics

Before you can prove a program does anything, you have to define how each operation transforms its state, that is, define its semantics. Most languages describe their semantics informally in prose, in a reference manual, and leave the concrete details to the compiler or interpreter implementation. A formal semantics writes the rules down in mathematics, precisely enough for a proof checker like Lean 4 to use them. Notable examples include CompCert’s semantics for C, CakeML’s for ML, and JSCert’s for JavaScript. Each one took years of expert effort, and often covers only a restricted subset of its language.

For this experiment we used an extended version of WHILE, the small imperative language used in textbooks such as Nielson and Nielson’s Semantics with Applications. Our version has integers, strings, first-class functions with closures, if, while and for loops, and runtime errors. Its interpreter is 1,855 lines of C, and a WHILE program looks like this (it prints 55):

var i = 0;
var sum = 0;
while (i < 10) {
    i = i + 1;
    sum = sum + i;
}
println(sum);

The semantics an LLM wrote for WHILE is a set of rules, one for each kind of expression and statement. These rules describe how to evaluate an expression in terms of its subexpressions. For integer addition, the rule is:

st, env ⊢ l ⇓ a, st'    st', env ⊢ r ⇓ b, st''    a + b = c
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                 st, env ⊢ l + r ⇓ c, st''

A rule reads from the bottom up. The line at the bottom is its conclusion. Starting from state st in environment env, the expression l + r evaluates (⇓) to c and leaves state st''. The state holds variable values, closures and everything printed so far; the environment says which variables are in scope. The premises above the line explain how the result follows from the subexpressions. First l evaluates to a, leaving state st'. Then r evaluates to b in that state, leaving st''. The final premise, a + b = c, adds the two integer values using WHILE’s 64-bit wrapping arithmetic.

Take (1 + 1) + x, with state [x ↦ 5] and environment {x}: x holds 5 and is in scope. Applying the rule gives:

[x ↦ 5], {x} ⊢ (1 + 1) ⇓ 2, [x ↦ 5]    [x ↦ 5], {x} ⊢ x ⇓ 5, [x ↦ 5]
                              2 + 5 = 7
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
              [x ↦ 5], {x} ⊢ (1 + 1) + x ⇓ 7, [x ↦ 5]

That is, to evaluate (1 + 1) + x, we first evaluate (1 + 1) to get 2, then look up x to get 5, and add the two values to get 7. Neither subexpression changes the state, so [x ↦ 5] remains unchanged.

To justify the first premise, we apply the addition rule again:

[x ↦ 5], {x} ⊢ 1 ⇓ 1, [x ↦ 5]    [x ↦ 5], {x} ⊢ 1 ⇓ 1, [x ↦ 5]
                           1 + 1 = 2
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
              [x ↦ 5], {x} ⊢ 1 + 1 ⇓ 2, [x ↦ 5]

These rule applications form a tree that derives the value of the whole expression from the values of its parts.

The LLM wrote about 400 lines of rules like these, in Lean (the full semantics). Each rule looks reasonable on its own, but an end user has no rigorous way to tell whether they faithfully describe how WHILE programs behave when they are actually run.

A semantics can pass every test and still be wrong

The usual way to check a semantics is to run it. Take a test suite, run each program under the semantics and under the real interpreter, and compare what they print. Unfortunately, in practice, this process is insufficient to build trust in the generated semantics.

For example, an early version of our semantics passed the test suite generated for the WHILE interpreter, but disagreed with the binary when a function’s name reached 59 characters:

fn aaa…aaa() {}           // a name of 59 a's
println("" + aaa…aaa);

semantics:  <fn aaa…aaa>
binary:     <fn aaa…aaa

The semantics said that concatenating a function with a string would include its full name between <fn and >. The binary dropped the closing >, and for longer names it dropped part of the name too. No test in the suite tried functions with names this long.

The reason is in the C interpreter that turns a value into a string when you concatenate it with +:

static char *stringify(Value v) {
    ...
    char buf[64];
    switch (v.kind) {
    ...
    case VAL_FN: {
        const char *name = v.as.fn->fn_expr->as.fn.name;
        if (name)
            snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "<fn %s>", name);
        else strcpy(buf, "<fn>");
        break;
    }
    default: strcpy(buf, "<native fn>"); break;
    }
    ...
}

stringify returns a string value as it is. Any other value is first printed into a 64-byte buffer on the stack and then copied into a freshly allocated string. A named closure is printed with snprintf as <fn name>, an anonymous one as <fn>, and the built-ins fall through to the default case, <native fn>.

snprintf writes at most 63 characters into the 64-byte buffer. The initial semantics used the same rendering rule for concatenation and printing, and missed this limit. To prove agreement with the binary, the LLM had to give concatenation its own renderer. The corrected semantics cuts a closure’s rendering to its first 63 bytes:

"" + f        ⇓  take 63 ("<fn " ++ f ++ ">")

This is the kind of detail an implementation accumulates internally but nobody writes down explicitly, which is precisely why a semantics transcribed by hand, or written by an LLM, can miss it. Nor is it a detail no program would notice: code in dynamic languages routinely relies on the string form of a function, for logging, for dispatch keyed on a name, or for comparing serialised values. Even simple violations like this undermine any verification effort built on top of the semantics, and can leave holes that hide security vulnerabilities. To build secure and scalable semantics, we need to go beyond tests, since a test suite only checks the programs someone (or an agent) thought to write.

Ship your interpreter

Shipping your interpreter means checking the semantics against the implementation people actually run. Compile the interpreter the language already has, and make the LLM prove that the binary refines the semantics, that is, that the two agree on what every program prints.

The theorem we proved is this one:

theorem endToEnd_refinement :
  ∀ p c, Loaded interpRunLayout p (fillZero c) →
    (∀ out, BigStep p out ↔ Halts c out 0) ∧
    (Diverges c → ¬ ∃ out, BigStep p out)

The theorem says for any WHILE program p, and any machine configuration c, if the machine configuration satisfies a property Loaded, then the semantics match what the compiled binary will do. Loaded interpRunLayout p (fillZero c) here says that c is a machine about to run p through the interpreter binary. The first conclusion, (∀ out, BigStep p out ↔ Halts c out 0), says that the semantics derives output out if and only if the machine halts with exit code 0 having printed out, i.e. for successfully terminating programs the predicted outputs are equivalent. The second says that any program p on which the machine runs forever (Diverges c), is a program the semantics derives no terminating output for.

We can visualise this theorem as a commuting square, showing how the semantics and the binary agree on a program’s output. In the diagram below, the top arrow relates a program p to the output out predicted by the semantics. The bottom arrow relates a machine state c to the output printed when the binary halts successfully. The dashed line on the left is the Loaded condition connecting the program to that machine state. Under this condition, the theorem says the two outputs agree, shown by the double line on the right. The orange arrow shows how a failed attempt to prove that agreement sends the LLM back to revise a rule of the semantics.

The theorem catches a wrong semantics in both directions. If the semantics is too permissive, it derives an output the binary never prints, and the left-to-right half fails. If it is too strict, it has no rule for something the binary does, and the right-to-left half fails. Either way the LLM gets a proof obligation it cannot discharge. In our experience, that obligation usually points at the rule that is wrong.

RISC-V is an open processor design. We use its formal model, written in Sail and translated into Lean, to define how each machine instruction executes. The binary is the actual ELF executable: 1,855 lines of interpreter C compiled by gcc, linked against dlmalloc and newlib, 25,336 instructions in all. For comparison, the xv6 kernel verified with MachCSL is 8,697 RISC-V instructions, built from 6,593 lines of C and assembly, although its proof also covers concurrency, which ours does not need. The C compiler’s output, the C library and the memory allocator are all inside our theorem. A person who wants to trust the result reads the statement above, the hypothesis Loaded, and the two short definitions of Halts and Diverges. They do not need to trust BigStep, because the proof checks it against the binary.

Developing the semantics and proof together

Developing the proof forced the LLMs to account for four details in the semantics:

  • integer arithmetic had to wrap at 64 bits, because negating the smallest integer was unsatisfiable against the machine;
  • a for loop’s initialiser had to ignore an abrupt status, because the C does;
  • built-ins had to render differently in print and in concatenation;
  • long closure names had to be cut at 63 bytes.

Each correction started either as an obligation that would not close or as a run of the binary that disagreed with the semantics.

The 63-byte cut is a representative example. The proof of the concatenation case needed the semantics’ rendering to equal the binary’s, and for long names it didn’t, so the obligation could not be discharged until the rule changed.

The proof also caught mistakes in the LLM-generated lemmas about the C library. The LLMs stated what each function does and then proved that statement against the machine code. An allocator reserve that no heap satisfied after a single malloc(24), a realloc lemma that was false for sizes that wrap, and an exit routine that writes errno without its lemma saying so all showed up the same way, as obligations that would not close.

Separation logic makes the binary proof tractable

LLMs wrote all of the proof. Most of the difficulty lay in reasoning about memory. We needed a specification for malloc, the function that allocates memory, which would let us prove that allocating a new block preserves the data already held by the interpreter. Even println("n = " + x) allocates three strings and frees two of them. Throughout those calls, the program’s variables and the half-built result must remain intact.

The textbook way to do this is to give each function a Hoare triple together with a footprint, a set of bytes the function may write. Facts about memory outside the footprint carry across a call unchanged. A triple { P } code { Q } reads as “if P holds before code runs, then Q holds after it”. For malloc, such a specification reads roughly as follows, where F is a fixed set of addresses:

{ heap H }
  p := malloc(n)
{ heap ((p, n) :: H)  and  p is fresh }
modifies F

Unfortunately, no such F exists. From the same heap, malloc(32) writes the header of the new top chunk at address 0x82000238, so F must contain that address. malloc(64) instead returns the block [0x82000210, 0x82000250), which contains it. Once the caller owns that block, facts about its bytes have to survive later calls, so F must also exclude 0x82000238. The LLMs proved in Lean that no fixed set of addresses can satisfy both requirements, after a first attempt that worked around the problem one fact at a time had stalled for three weeks.

Separation logic solves this by making the footprint depend on the heap. We ported MachCSL, the logic behind the xv6 proof, to the newly released iris-lean.1 In separation logic the allocator owns the free bytes of its arena, and malloc’s specification hands part of them to the caller:

{ isHeap H }
  p := malloc(n)
{ (p = 0 ∗ isHeap H)
  ∨ (isHeap ((p, n) :: H) ∗ blockOwn p n) }

Here ∗ is the separating conjunction, which says that its two halves hold of disjoint parts of memory, and the result p is either null or a fresh block. isHeap H owns every byte of the arena outside the live blocks H. Initially, the allocator owns 0x82000238, so malloc(32) may write it. If the caller instead requests malloc(64), that byte passes to the caller through blockOwn, and later calls cannot touch it. Anything else the caller owns is not mentioned in the specification, and the frame rule carries it across the call in one step. After the port, the rest of the proof closed in a few days.

At its peak the proof was about a million lines of Lean, two thirds of it generated by 35 scripts the LLMs wrote, which read the binary and emit a proof rule for each of about 11,800 instructions. A later pass replaced the generated proof families with abstractions proved once, such as a symbolic executor for machine code, and brought the proof under 200,000 lines. It uses no axioms beyond Lean’s standard ones (propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound).

The theorem applies to real programs

A theorem with a hypothesis is only useful if that hypothesis can be satisfied. If Loaded described a machine state that never occurs, our theorem would hold vacuously and tell us nothing about the binary.

We had the LLMs prove in Lean that Loaded holds for ten programs. For each one, they constructed a machine state at the interpreter’s entry, with the program in memory alongside the binary, the runtime and the allocator. Lean checked that each state met the theorem’s precondition.2

We also replayed 85,483 machine steps from the executable and checked that the resulting memory matched the constructed state byte for byte. The link from the executable file and its boot trace to that state was checked by scripts; Lean checked the precondition and the execution from that state onwards. For the full loop test program, which extends the earlier example with two more sums, the binary provably halts after printing 55, 2500 and 36 on separate lines.

The precondition includes enough heap and stack space for the program. A later theorem replaces these two assumptions with checkers that run on the program.

Once you trust the semantics, the tools are cheap

A validated semantics also works as an interface. Anything you prove sound against BigStep is sound for the binary, by composing it with the refinement theorem, and that composition is a few lines of Lean. So we had LLMs build four tools on top of it.

The refinement proof took about a month and is about 140,000 lines of Lean. The four tools below were opened as pull requests over three days, and come to about 33,000 lines between them, most of it the compiler.

The first tool is a type checker. It catches invalid operations before a program runs. For example, these two programs are rejected:

"a" - 1;               // subtracting an integer from a string

var x = 1;
x = "s";               // assigning a string to an integer variable

The proofs for these examples show that neither program can pass the checker. Its soundness theorem rules out type errors in accepted programs, including when they run through the interpreter binary. Division by zero, a failed assert and the interpreter’s call-depth limit remain possible; those require reasoning about values as well as types.

The second tool is a program logic, which lets us prove what a particular program computes. The loop near the start of this post adds the integers from 1 to 10. The full test program also adds the odd integers from 1 to 100, using break and continue, and computes a third sum with nested loops. The LLMs used the logic to prove that running this program through the interpreter binary terminates and prints exactly:

55
2500
36

The third tool is an abstract interpreter, an analysis that tracks possible values through a program and raises alarms for potential runtime errors. It analyses that same test program with no alarms, proving it free of runtime errors. It also establishes that the final values of sum, total and acc are 55, 2500 and 36. The analysis computes these results automatically, and its soundness proof connects them to execution of the binary.

The fourth tool does without the interpreter entirely. In April, our agents built a compiler but could not prove it correct. Here the semantics came first, and the LLMs built a verified compiler from all of WHILE (strings, closures, calls, for, return and assert) straight to RISC-V. Compile the sum program above, and the resulting machine code prints the same three numbers. The correctness theorem establishes agreement for every program meeting its preconditions. A checked version analyses allocation cost, so its theorem needs no assumption about available heap space.

Dropping the interpreter also makes WHILE programs faster. We ran every program in the interpreter’s test suite both ways on the spike RISC-V simulator. Counting the interpreter from the moment it starts evaluating, so that parsing is not charged against it, compiled code retires between 2.7 and 8.2 times fewer instructions, and both routes print the same output. These are instruction counts on a simulator rather than timings on hardware.

Once the semantics is trusted, it is the language, and the binary we started from is no longer needed to run WHILE programs.

What’s next: Lua, OCaml and, one day, CPython

Our experiment with WHILE targeted a toy language. LLMs developed its formal semantics, proved that the compiled interpreter follows it, and built verified tools on top. We are now scaling this approach up to real languages.

Ship your Lua targets Lua 5.4.7 compiled to bare-metal RISC-V. The binary already runs on the Sail model and agrees with native Lua, and the plan cuts the proof at the VM: first the bytecode interpreter against a bytecode semantics, fragment by fragment over opcodes, then the source language against the bytecode.

Ship your OCaml takes advantage of the way OCaml bootstraps itself. OCaml’s bootstrap compiler is checked into its repository as bytecode, boot/ocamlc, and runs on ocamlrun. We have ocamlrun running on the Sail model, compiling programs with the real boot/ocamlc. The plan there ends in a fixpoint: if the source semantics says the compiler compiles its own sources to exactly the bytes of boot/ocamlc, and the compiler’s back end is proved correct, then those bytes get a meaning without verifying their 412,000 bytecode instructions one at a time.

For both projects, we have already stated the headline theorems in Lean. What remains is to close their proofs.

The north star is CPython. We believe that current agents make an LLM-written, machine-validated semantics for Python feasible, given enough compute. Tools like the ones in the previous section could then be built on it, with guarantees that reach the CPython binary.

Compile the interpreter the language already has, and make the LLM prove that the binary refines the semantics, that is, that the two agree on what every program prints.The theorem we proved is this one:theorem endToEnd_refinement : ∀ p c, Loaded interpRunLayout p (fillZero c) → (∀ out, BigStep p out ↔ Halts c out 0) ∧ (Diverges c → ¬ ∃ out, BigStep p out) The theorem says for any WHILE program p, and any machine configuration c, if the machine configuration satisfies a property Loaded, then the semantics match what the compiled binary will do. Loaded interpRunLayout p (fillZero c) here says that c is a machine about to run p through the interpreter binary. The first conclusion, (∀ out, BigStep p out ↔ Halts c out 0), says that the semantics derives output out if and only if the machine halts with exit code 0 having printed out, i.e. for successfully terminating programs the predicted outputs are equivalent. The second says that any program p on which the machine runs forever (Diverges c), is a program the semantics derives no terminating output for.We can visualise this theorem as a commuting square, showing how the semantics and the binary agree on a program’s output. In the diagram below, the top arrow relates a program p to the output out predicted by the semantics. The bottom arrow relates a machine state c to the output printed when the binary halts successfully. The dashed line on the left is the Loaded condition connecting the program to that machine state. Under this condition, the theorem says the two outputs agree, shown by the double line on the right. The orange arrow shows how a failed attempt to prove that agreement sends the LLM back to revise a rule of the semantics.For a program loaded into the machine, the semantics and successful execution agree on the output.The theorem catches a wrong semantics in both directions. If the semantics is too permissive, it derives an output the binary never prints, and the left-to-right half fails. If it is too strict, it has no rule for something the binary does, and the right-to-left half fails. Either way the LLM gets a proof obligation it cannot discharge. In our experience, that obligation usually points at the rule that is wrong.RISC-V is an open processor design. We use its formal model, written in Sail and translated into Lean, to define how each machine instruction executes. The binary is the actual ELF executable: 1,855 lines of interpreter C compiled by gcc, linked against dlmalloc and newlib, 25,336 instructions in all. For comparison, the xv6 kernel verified with MachCSL is 8,697 RISC-V instructions, built from 6,593 lines of C and assembly, although its proof also covers concurrency, which ours does not need. The C compiler’s output, the C library and the memory allocator are all inside our theorem. A person who wants to trust the result reads the statement above, the hypothesis Loaded, and the two short definitions of Halts and Diverges. They do not need to trust BigStep, because the proof checks it against the binary.Developing the semantics and proof togetherDeveloping the proof forced the LLMs to account for four details in the semantics:integer arithmetic had to wrap at 64 bits, because negating the smallest integer was unsatisfiable against the machine;a for loop’s initialiser had to ignore an abrupt status, because the C does;built-ins had to render differently in print and in concatenation;long closure names had to be cut at 63 bytes.Each correction started either as an obligation that would not close or as a run of the binary that disagreed with the semantics.The 63-byte cut is a representative example. The proof of the concatenation case needed the semantics’ rendering to equal the binary’s, and for long names it didn’t, so the obligation could not be discharged until the rule changed.The proof also caught mistakes in the LLM-generated lemmas about the C library. The LLMs stated what each function does and then proved that statement against the machine code. An allocator reserve that no heap satisfied after a single malloc(24), a realloc lemma that was false for sizes that wrap, and an exit routine that writes errno without its lemma saying so all showed up the same way, as obligations that would not close.Separation logic makes the binary proof tractableLLMs wrote all of the proof. Most of the difficulty lay in reasoning about memory. We needed a specification for malloc, the function that allocates memory, which would let us prove that allocating a new block preserves the data already held by the interpreter. Even println("n = " + x) allocates three strings and frees two of them. Throughout those calls, the program’s variables and the half-built result must remain intact.The textbook way to do this is to give each function a Hoare triple together with a footprint, a set of bytes the function may write. Facts about memory outside the footprint carry across a call unchanged. A triple { P } code { Q } reads as “if P holds before code runs, then Q holds after it”. For malloc, such a specification reads roughly as follows, where F is a fixed set of addresses:{ heap H } p := malloc(n) { heap ((p, n) :: H) and p is fresh } modifies F Unfortunately, no such F exists. From the same heap, malloc(32) writes the header of the new top chunk at address 0x82000238, so F must contain that address. malloc(64) instead returns the block [0x82000210, 0x82000250), which contains it. Once the caller owns that block, facts about its bytes have to survive later calls, so F must also exclude 0x82000238. The LLMs proved in Lean that no fixed set of addresses can satisfy both requirements, after a first attempt that worked around the problem one fact at a time had stalled for three weeks.From the same heap, malloc(32) writes a byte that malloc(64) would hand to the caller. The allocator's write footprint must change as ownership of memory changes.Separation logic solves this by making the footprint depend on the heap. We ported MachCSL, the logic behind the xv6 proof, to the newly released iris-lean.1 In separation logic the allocator owns the free bytes of its arena, and malloc’s specification hands part of them to the caller:{ isHeap H } p := malloc(n) { (p = 0 ∗ isHeap H) ∨ (isHeap ((p, n) :: H) ∗ blockOwn p n) } Here ∗ is the separating conjunction, which says that its two halves hold of disjoint parts of memory, and the result p is either null or a fresh block. isHeap H owns every byte of the arena outside the live blocks H. Initially, the allocator owns 0x82000238, so malloc(32) may write it. If the caller instead requests malloc(64), that byte passes to the caller through blockOwn, and later calls cannot touch it. Anything else the caller owns is not mentioned in the specification, and the frame rule carries it across the call in one step. After the port, the rest of the proof closed in a few days.LLMs write the semantics and the proof linking it to the existing interpreter binary; Lean checks that proof against the machine model.At its peak the proof was about a million lines of Lean, two thirds of it generated by 35 scripts the LLMs wrote, which read the binary and emit a proof rule for each of about 11,800 instructions. A later pass replaced the generated proof families with abstractions proved once, such as a symbolic executor for machine code, and brought the proof under 200,000 lines. It uses no axioms beyond Lean’s standard ones (propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound).The theorem applies to real programsA theorem with a hypothesis is only useful if that hypothesis can be satisfied. If Loaded described a machine state that never occurs, our theorem would hold vacuously and tell us nothing about the binary.We had the LLMs prove in Lean that Loaded holds for ten programs. For each one, they constructed a machine state at the interpreter’s entry, with the program in memory alongside the binary, the runtime and the allocator. Lean checked that each state met the theorem’s precondition.2Loaded specifies the memory and registers needed to run the program through the interpreter binary. The program enters as a syntax tree (orange); the surrounding code and runtime state come from the interpreter.We also replayed 85,483 machine steps from the executable and checked that the resulting memory matched the constructed state byte for byte. The link from the executable file and its boot trace to that state was checked by scripts; Lean checked the precondition and the execution from that state onwards. For the full loop test program, which extends the earlier example with two more sums, the binary provably halts after printing 55, 2500 and 36 on separate lines.The precondition includes enough heap and stack space for the program. A later theorem replaces these two assumptions with checkers that run on the program.Once you trust the semantics, the tools are cheapA validated semantics also works as an interface. Anything you prove sound against BigStep is sound for the binary, by composing it with the refinement theorem, and that composition is a few lines of Lean. So we had LLMs build four tools on top of it.The type system, program logic and analyser reuse the interpreter's refinement proof. The compiler is proved to implement the same semantics directly on RISC-V.The refinement proof took about a month and is about 140,000 lines of Lean. The four tools below were opened as pull requests over three days, and come to about 33,000 lines between them, most of it the compiler.The first tool is a type checker. It catches invalid operations before a program runs. For example, these two programs are rejected:"a" - 1; // subtracting an integer from a string var x = 1; x = "s"; // assigning a string to an integer variable The proofs for these examples show that neither program can pass the checker. Its soundness theorem rules out type errors in accepted programs, including when they run through the interpreter binary. Division by zero, a failed assert and the interpreter’s call-depth limit remain possible; those require reasoning about values as well as types.The second tool is a program logic, which lets us prove what a particular program computes. The loop near the start of this post adds the integers from 1 to 10. The full test program also adds the odd integers from 1 to 100, using break and continue, and computes a third sum with nested loops. The LLMs used the logic to prove that running this program through the interpreter binary terminates and prints exactly:55 2500 36 The third tool is an abstract interpreter, an analysis that tracks possible values through a program and raises alarms for potential runtime errors. It analyses that same test program with no alarms, proving it free of runtime errors. It also establishes that the final values of sum, total and acc are 55, 2500 and 36. The analysis computes these results automatically, and its soundness proof connects them to execution of the binary.The fourth tool does without the interpreter entirely. In April, our agents built a compiler but could not prove it correct. Here the semantics came first, and the LLMs built a verified compiler from all of WHILE (strings, closures, calls, for, return and assert) straight to RISC-V. Compile the sum program above, and the resulting machine code prints the same three numbers. The correctness theorem establishes agreement for every program meeting its preconditions. A checked version analyses allocation cost, so its theorem needs no assumption about available heap space.Dropping the interpreter also makes WHILE programs faster. We ran every program in the interpreter’s test suite both ways on the spike RISC-V simulator. Counting the interpreter from the moment it starts evaluating, so that parsing is not charged against it, compiled code retires between 2.7 and 8.2 times fewer instructions, and both routes print the same output. These are instruction counts on a simulator rather than timings on hardware.Compiling these WHILE programs reduces instruction counts by a factor of 2.7–8.2 while preserving their output. Counts come from the spike RISC-V simulator and exclude parsing by the interpreter.Once the semantics is trusted, it is the language, and the binary we started from is no longer needed to run WHILE programs.What’s next: Lua, OCaml and, one day, CPythonOur experiment with WHILE targeted a toy language. LLMs developed its formal semantics, proved that the compiled interpreter follows it, and built verified tools on top. We are now scaling this approach up to real languages.Ship your Lua targets Lua 5.4.7 compiled to bare-metal RISC-V. The binary already runs on the Sail model and agrees with native Lua, and the plan cuts the proof at the VM: first the bytecode interpreter against a bytecode semantics, fragment by fragment over opcodes, then the source language against the bytecode.Ship your OCaml takes advantage of the way OCaml bootstraps itself. OCaml’s bootstrap compiler is checked into its repository as bytecode, boot/ocamlc, and runs on ocamlrun. We have ocamlrun running on the Sail model, compiling programs with the real boot/ocamlc. The plan there ends in a fixpoint: if the source semantics says the compiler compiles its own sources to exactly the bytes of boot/ocamlc, and the compiler’s back end is proved correct, then those bytes get a meaning without verifying their 412,000 bytecode instructions one at a time.For both projects, we have already stated the headline theorems in Lean. What remains is to close their proofs.The north star is CPython. We believe that current agents make an LLM-written, machine-validated semantics for Python feasible, given enough compute. Tools like the ones in the previous section could then be built on it, with guarantees that reach the CPython binary.The project was genuinely stuck before iris-lean came out. blocks.html_en: To prove anything about a program, we first need a mathematical description of what it does. This starts with describing the programming language it is written in: what every statement, loop, and function call means when it runs. These descriptions are called a formal semantics, and can be written with pen and paper, but are increasingly expressed in a proof assistant such as Lean. A handful of languages have one (Standard ML, WebAssembly, and C via CompCert), as does the RISC-V instruction set that a growing number of processors execute. Developing each of these semantics took years of expert effort.

blocks.html_en: Languages without a formal semantics still have interpreters or compilers, which in practice define what their programs mean. Here we consider a radical idea: make the LLM prove that its semantics agrees with the real interpreter on every program, treating the interpreter as ground truth. To do this, we compile the interpreter to RISC-V, whose meaning is already formally defined. That gives an exact, if unreadable, description of what the interpreter does with any program. The LLM then writes readable rules for the language and proves in Lean that, for every possible program, those rules predict exactly what the compiled interpreter prints. If a rule is wrong, the proof gets stuck.

blocks.html_en: The theorem catches a wrong semantics in both directions. If the semantics is too permissive, it derives an output the binary never prints, and the left-to-right half fails. If it is too strict, it has no rule for something the binary does, and the right-to-left half fails. Either way the LLM gets a proof obligation it cannot discharge. In our experience, that obligation usually points at the rule that is wrong.

blocks.html_en: RISC-V is an open processor design. We use its formal model, written in Sail and translated into Lean, to define how each machine instruction executes. The binary is the actual ELF executable: 1,855 lines of interpreter C compiled by gcc, linked against dlmalloc and newlib, 25,336 instructions in all. For comparison, the xv6 kernel verified with MachCSL is 8,697 RISC-V instructions, built from 6,593 lines of C and assembly, although its proof also covers concurrency, which ours does not need. The C compiler’s output, the C library and the memory allocator are all inside our theorem. A person who wants to trust the result reads the statement above, the hypothesis Loaded, and the two short definitions of Halts and Diverges. They do not need to trust BigStep, because the proof checks it against the binary.

blocks.html_en: Unfortunately, no such F exists. From the same heap, malloc(32) writes the header of the new top chunk at address 0x82000238, so F must contain that address. malloc(64) instead returns the block [0x82000210, 0x82000250), which contains it. Once the caller owns that block, facts about its bytes have to survive later calls, so F must also exclude 0x82000238. The LLMs proved in Lean that no fixed set of addresses can satisfy both requirements, after a first attempt that worked around the problem one fact at a time had stalled for three weeks.

blocks.html_en: Here ∗ is the separating conjunction, which says that its two halves hold of disjoint parts of memory, and the result p is either null or a fresh block. isHeap H owns every byte of the arena outside the live blocks H. Initially, the allocator owns 0x82000238, so malloc(32) may write it. If the caller instead requests malloc(64), that byte passes to the caller through blockOwn, and later calls cannot touch it.
